Brain Fog: Eight Treatable Causes to Rule Out First

By Adam Seay, D.C., Root Health, Garner, NC. Updated October 2, 2026.

The short answer

Brain fog is one of the least specific symptoms in medicine. That cuts both ways. It gets brushed off as stress or age, and it very often comes from something common, testable and fixable: low B12, a thyroid problem, sleep apnea, anemia, a medication side effect, hearing loss or blood sugar. Check those first, before any supplement.

Get same-day medical care, not a reading list, for confusion or memory loss that comes on over hours to days, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, sudden vision loss, a severe headache unlike any before, confusion with fever or after a head injury or fall, or a sudden change in thinking after starting or changing a medication. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988, any time. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911.

You walk into a room and forget why. A word you have used a thousand times will not come. You read a paragraph three times and cannot say what it said. If you took this to a doctor, you may have heard that your labs are normal. Sometimes that is the whole answer. Often it is not, because a standard panel checks a narrow set of things and stops there.

Eight treatable causes

1. Low B12 or folate

B12 deficiency causes well-documented problems with mood, memory and slowed thinking.1 It is common in older adults, people on long-term acid reducers, strict vegans and vegetarians, and after some weight-loss surgeries. Ask for B12 with methylmalonic acid, the more sensitive marker, and folate measured in red blood cells if possible.

2. Thyroid problems

Hypothyroidism, overt or subclinical, is a recognized cause of brain fog, often before the diagnosis is made.2 To be fair to the data, a large pooled analysis of more than 74,000 adults did not find measurable differences on cognitive tests with milder, subclinical thyroid changes.3 Both can be true. A TSH and free T4 are cheap, and correcting a genuinely abnormal level is safe and often helps.

3. Sleep apnea

Loud snoring, pauses in breathing, waking up gasping and daytime sleepiness are reasons to ask about a sleep study. In a study of nearly 2,800 middle-aged adults, self-reported sleep apnea was linked to poorer memory.4 It is also very treatable.

4. Anemia

Less hemoglobin means less oxygen reaching the brain. In hospitalized older adults, each 1 g/dL drop in hemoglobin was tied to a meaningfully worse score on a standard cognitive screen.5 A CBC and ferritin catch most of it.

5. Low vitamin D and B vitamins

Low vitamin D and low intake of several B vitamins have been linked to depressive symptoms, though supplement trials for mood have been inconsistent.6 The fair summary is to check and correct if low, not to expect a cure.

6. Medications, including over-the-counter ones

Drugs with anticholinergic effects, including some allergy pills, bladder medications, older antidepressants and sleep aids, are linked to measurable cognitive impairment, especially as they add up.7 Bring your full list, supplements included, and ask about anticholinergic burden. Do not stop a prescription on your own.

7. Hearing loss

This one surprises people. The Lancet Commission on dementia named midlife hearing loss one of the largest potentially modifiable risk factors.8 A U.S. analysis estimated that about 17 percent of dementia cases among adults with moderate or greater measured hearing loss were attributable to it.9 A hearing screen is quick and painless.

8. Blood sugar

The brain is very sensitive to blood sugar and insulin. Type 2 diabetes is increasingly recognized as a risk factor for cognitive decline, through inflammation, impaired insulin signaling in the brain and other routes.10 If your fog is worse after meals or better with regular eating, ask for fasting glucose, A1c and fasting insulin.

If gut symptoms come with the fog

Bloating, irregular bowels, reflux or food reactions alongside brain fog are worth raising on their own, because the gut and brain are in constant contact and gut-focused testing may be relevant. One caution: urine neurotransmitter tests measure real chemicals, but most of what they measure comes from the gut, adrenal glands and nerves outside the brain. A review of their validity found the strongest established use is detecting a rare adrenal tumor, not judging mood or cognition.11 Treat any result as one data point, not a reading of your brain chemistry.

On psychiatric medication. If you take an antidepressant or another psychiatric medication, do not stop or change it on your own. Withdrawal symptoms are common when antidepressants are stopped, about 43 percent in one large analysis.12 Any change belongs with your prescriber.

Common questions

What blood tests should I ask for with brain fog?

A reasonable first set: CBC and ferritin, B12 with methylmalonic acid, folate, TSH and free T4, vitamin D, fasting glucose, A1c and fasting insulin. Add a hearing screen, and if you snore, a conversation about a sleep study.

Do supplements help brain fog?

Only when they correct something you are actually short on. Finding one reversible cause on the list above is worth more than months of supplements aimed at the wrong problem. Be careful with St. John's wort and 5-HTP if you take an antidepressant; both can interact dangerously with it.

Is brain fog a sign of dementia?

Usually not, and most brain fog builds gradually from common causes like the ones above. Sudden or rapidly worsening confusion is different and needs same-day care. If you are worried about steady decline in memory, that belongs with your physician and, if needed, a neurologist.
